newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Suharto's daughter says her father in good health.
newsitem.headline: Suharto's daughter says her father in good health.

text.p: The eldest daughter of Indonesia's long-ruling President Suharto said her father was in good health, as debate over his future plans and who will succeed him continued in the run-up to May 29 general elections.
"Thank God, he is still healthy," Siti Hardiyanti Rukmana told Reuters on Sunday night in an interview on the campaign trail in central Java.

Suharto, aged 75 and now the world's second-longest ruling leader after Cuba's Fidel Castro, underwent a thorough medical checkup in Germany in mid-1996 and was given a clean bill of health for a man of his age.
Financial markets have been spooked in recent months, however, on unfounded rumours on the health of the president, who has ruled Indonesia for 30 years.

The question of who will eventually succeed the former army general as president is one of the key issues facing Indonesia. Suharto is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term in office in presidential polls next March.
Major policy moves and government changes normally follow the presidential election, rather than the general elections.
"When it comes to questions whether he is ready or not to be re-appointed as the president, it will depend on the Indonesian people," his daughter Rukmana said.
Juwono Sudarsono, professor of politics at the University of Indonesia, said there was some uncertainty over the country's political future because it had been dominated by Suharto for so long.
"Some people are worried about the absence of institutionalised and organised work below the presidency in case something happens to the president," he told Reuters recently.
Rukmana, 48, also known as Tutut, is a successful busineswoman and one of seven chairpersons of the ruling Golkar, one of three parties legally permitted to contest the general elections.
Her name has surfaced as a possible vice president but she avoided any direct comment on her political future.
"It will be up to the Indonesian people, beccause there is a mechanism that is through the representatives. I can't answer the question because the election is not over yet," she said.

Some analysts suggest that Tutut, who is proving to be one of the most effective campaigners for Golkar, is being groomed to become overall head of the party, rather than vice-president of the nation.

The president and vice president are elected every five years by the People's Consultative Assembly, made up of the 500 members of the parliamentary House of Representatives and 500 government-appointed members.
Some political analysts believe current Vice President Try Sutrisno may be re-elected, although Suharto has never had a two-term vice president during his 30-year rule.
The vice-presidential post is under keen scrutiny, given Suharto's age and the possibility that his next running mate may become president.
